- Evaluate each CV independently against only the listed criteria — do not compare CVs to each other or rank them.
- Do not factor in name, presumed gender, age, nationality, employment gaps (unless directly relevant to a stated criterion), or school prestige beyond confirming a required degree.
- For each CV, rate every criterion as "Matches," "Partial match," "Does not match," or "Insufficient information," quoting the CV as evidence.
- End each CV's summary with: "This is a structured comparison to support human review, not a hiring recommendation. A human should make the final screening decision."

variations.label: Screening with a required certification or hard credential
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the role has one non-negotiable, verifiable credential (a license, a certification, a legal work-authorization requirement) that should be checked distinctly from softer experience criteria.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me screen a CV against role criteria. This is a triage aid only — not a hiring decision.

Role: [TITLE]
Required credential (hard gate — must be explicitly present): [CREDENTIAL, e.g. "active RN license," "CPA certification"]
Other must-have criteria: [LIST]
Nice-to-have criteria: [LIST]
CV content: [PASTE CV TEXT — role-relevant content only]

Rules:
- Check the required credential first and separately, stating clearly whether it's explicitly present, explicitly absent, or not mentioned (which should be treated as "insufficient information," not "does not match," since it may simply not have been listed).
- Evaluate all other criteria as "Matches / Partial match / Does not match / Insufficient information," with no factoring in of name, age, gender, nationality, or unrelated gaps.
- End with the required human-review disclaimer, verbatim: "This is a structured comparison to support human review, not a hiring recommendation. A human should make the final screening decision, especially for any 'insufficient information' or 'partial match' result."

variations.label: Re-screen after updating criteria mid-search
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you've refined your criteria partway through a search (a common and reasonable thing to do) and need to re-screen CVs you already looked at under the old criteria, to keep the process fair across all candidates.
variations.prompt:
I'm re-screening a CV I looked at earlier because our role criteria have been updated since then. Treat this as a fresh evaluation, not influenced by any prior read.

Role: [TITLE]
Updated must-have criteria: [LIST]
Updated nice-to-have criteria: [LIST]
CV content: [PASTE CV TEXT — role-relevant content only]

Rules: same as the standard screening prompt — per-criterion ratings only, no factoring in of name/age/gender/nationality/unrelated gaps/school prestige, evidence quoted from the CV, and the standard human-review disclaimer at the end. Note explicitly that this is a re-screen under updated criteria, in case the earlier read needs to be revisited too for fairness.

followUps.label: Push back on a rating that seems to have drifted
followUps.prompt: Re-check the rating for [CRITERION NAME] — it's marked as [CURRENT RATING], but I want you to justify that strictly against the exact wording of the CV and the criterion, quoting the specific text. If the quoted evidence doesn't clearly support that rating, change it and explain why.

followUps.label: Confirm no excluded factors leaked in
followUps.prompt: Go back through your evaluation and confirm explicitly that none of the ratings were influenced by the candidate's name, presumed gender, age, nationality, employment gaps unrelated to a stated criterion, or school prestige beyond the required degree. If any rating might have been affected by one of these, re-evaluate it using only the stated criteria.

followUps.label: Turn an 'insufficient information' flag into a clarifying question
followUps.prompt: For every criterion marked 'insufficient information,' draft one short, specific, job-relevant question I could send the candidate to clarify it directly, rather than assuming the worst.

followUps.label: Spot-check against your own independent read
followUps.prompt: Before I look at this myself, tell me which rating in this summary you're least confident about and why — I want to focus my own independent read on exactly that part of the CV.

hr-i1-screen-cvs-against-criteria-fairly.walkthrough:
Fatima is hiring a mid-level Project Manager and, before looking at a single CV, writes down her real criteria: must-have is 3+ years leading cross-functional projects and experience with a named PM methodology; nice-to-have is a PMP certification and client-services background.

She opens Claude and pastes the CV-screening prompt for the first candidate, with the role, her criteria, and the CV's relevant content (redacting the candidate's photo and graduation year before pasting, since her team's process calls for that).

Claude returns a per-criterion comparison: "Cross-functional project experience: Matches — CV states '4 years coordinating cross-functional launches across engineering and marketing.'" and "PM methodology: Insufficient information — CV does not mention a specific methodology; worth asking directly rather than assuming absence." No mention of the candidate's name, age, or any employment gap appears anywhere in the output, and the required disclaimer is present at the end, stating a human must make the final call.

Fatima wants to be sure the "insufficient information" flag on methodology wasn't secretly influenced by something else in the CV, so she sends the follow-up: "Confirm none of these ratings were influenced by name, age, gender, nationality, unrelated gaps, or school prestige — if any might have been, re-evaluate using only the stated criteria." Claude confirms the methodology rating was based purely on the absence of that specific term in the CV text, not on anything else.

Rather than treating the missing methodology info as a soft rejection, Fatima drafts a short clarifying question to send the candidate directly, using Claude's suggested wording, and makes her actual advance decision herself once she has the answer. Total time: about 10 minutes per CV, including the clarifying question.

placeholders.name: e.g., remote work, PTO, expense reimbursement
placeholders.what: The specific policy topic this document covers — one topic at a time, not a bundle of several policies in one document, which gets confusing for employees to reference.
examples: remote work policy
paid time off (PTO) policy
expense reimbursement policy

placeholders.name: PASTE DECISIONS, e.g., "employees may work remote up to 3 days/week, manager approval required, must be reachable during core hours 10am-3pm local time"
placeholders.what: The actual policy decisions that have already been made by HR leadership, legal, or founders — real, confirmed rules, not your own guess at what the policy should be. This document turns decisions into documentation; it doesn't make the decisions.
examples: employees may work remote up to 3 days per week, manager approval required in advance, must be reachable during core hours 10am-3pm in their local time zone, exceptions require director-level sign-off

full-time employees accrue 15 PTO days per year starting day one, prorated for partial first year, unused days roll over up to 5 days into the next year, requests need 2 weeks notice except for emergencies

expenses under $50 can be self-approved and submitted via the expense app within 30 days, expenses over $50 require manager pre-approval, reimbursement is processed within 10 business days of submission

placeholders.name: PASTE, e.g., how to request, who approves, what system to use
placeholders.what: The real, current process steps — which system employees use, who approves what, and any timing requirements. If the process doesn't actually work this way in practice, the document will create confusion the moment someone follows it exactly as written and it doesn't match reality.
examples: Request via the HR portal at least 1 week in advance for planned remote days; manager approves or denies within 2 business days; recurring arrangements get reviewed quarterly.
Submit PTO requests through the HR system; direct manager approves within 3 business days; HR is cc'd automatically and updates the shared team calendar.
Submit receipts through the expense app within 30 days of purchase; manager approval required for anything over $50; finance processes approved reimbursements on the next bi-weekly pay cycle.

placeholders.name: e.g., all employees / a specific team
placeholders.what: Who this policy applies to — everyone at the company, or a specific team, level, or employment type (full-time only, a specific office location). Scope matters because a policy written for "all employees" that actually only applies to one team will confuse people it doesn't apply to.
examples: all full-time employees
all employees except those in roles requiring on-site presence (listed separately)
employees at the headquarters office only; other locations follow local policy

variations.label: FAQ-format version for a policy with common questions
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a policy that tends to generate a lot of similar employee questions, so the documentation format itself answers likely questions upfront.
variations.prompt:
Draft an FAQ-format HR policy document from the decisions below. Use only what I state — do not invent legal requirements or jurisdiction-specific rules.

Policy topic: [e.g., remote work, PTO, expense reimbursement]
Our actual policy decisions: [PASTE DECISIONS]
Process steps involved: [PASTE PROCESS STEPS]
Common questions employees are likely to ask: [LIST 3-5, e.g. "what happens if I need more remote days for a specific reason," "does unused time roll over"]
Audience: [e.g., all employees]

Rules: same as the standard policy prompt — plain language, no invented legal claims, jurisdiction-specific gaps listed under "Needs legal/compliance review" rather than filled with generic language, clear process section, effective-date placeholder at the end. Format as question-and-answer pairs covering the listed questions plus the core policy.

variations.label: Policy update / redline version
variations.whenToUse: Use this when revising an existing policy rather than writing one from scratch, so the changes are clearly visible against the prior version.
variations.prompt:
I'm updating an existing HR policy. Draft the revised employee-facing documentation and clearly show what changed from the previous version. Use only what I state — do not invent legal requirements.

Policy topic: [e.g., remote work]
Previous policy decisions: [PASTE OLD DECISIONS]
New/updated policy decisions: [PASTE NEW DECISIONS]
Reason for the change, if useful to share with employees: [1 SENTENCE, OR "not sharing a reason"]
Process steps involved (updated): [PASTE]
Audience: [e.g., all employees]

Write: 1) the full revised policy in plain language, 2) a short "What's changing" summary highlighting just the differences from the old policy, 3) the standard "Needs legal/compliance review" section for anything jurisdiction-specific, 4) an effective-date placeholder: [EFFECTIVE DATE].

variations.label: Manager-facing companion guide (separate from the employee policy)
variations.whenToUse: Use this to create a second, manager-only document explaining how to apply and enforce a policy consistently, alongside the employee-facing version.
variations.prompt:
Draft a manager-facing companion guide for applying the HR policy below consistently. Use only what I state — do not invent legal requirements or guidance beyond what's given.

Policy topic: [e.g., remote work]
The employee-facing policy (for reference): [PASTE THE EMPLOYEE-FACING POLICY TEXT]
Common edge cases managers are likely to face: [LIST, e.g. "an employee asks for a 4th remote day for a one-time reason," "a request comes in with less than the required notice"]

Write guidance for each edge case grounded only in the stated policy — where the policy doesn't clearly cover a case, say so explicitly and note it should go to HR rather than a manager's own judgment. Flag anywhere managers might be tempted to apply the policy inconsistently, and give a one-line rule to prevent that.

followUps.label: Escalate a jurisdiction-specific claim to real legal review
followUps.prompt: Look again at everything under 'Needs legal/compliance review' and, for each item, tell me specifically what question I need to ask our legal or compliance contact — phrase each as a direct question I can send them, not just a vague flag.

followUps.label: Check no legal-sounding language snuck into the policy body
followUps.prompt: Re-read the policy body itself (not the flagged section) and check for any sentence that sounds like it's stating a legal entitlement or requirement, even if it wasn't explicitly flagged. Move anything you find into the 'Needs legal/compliance review' section instead.

followUps.label: Process doesn't match reality — fix it
followUps.prompt: The process section says [DESCRIBE WHAT'S WRONG, e.g. 'approval happens within 2 business days'], but that's not actually how it works today — it's closer to [ACTUAL PROCESS]. Update the process section to match what actually happens, not the aspirational version.

followUps.label: Simplify for employees who'll skim, not read closely
followUps.prompt: Most employees will skim this, not read closely. Add a 3-bullet 'the short version' summary at the very top, above the full policy, covering just the most important practical points.

hr-i2-hr-policy-and-process-documentatio.walkthrough:
Tobias is documenting his company's remote work policy after leadership finalized the actual decisions: up to 3 remote days per week, manager approval required in advance, and reachability required during core hours 10am-3pm local time. No jurisdiction-specific detail was discussed.

He opens ChatGPT and pastes the policy documentation prompt: topic (remote work), the real decisions exactly as leadership stated them, the process (request via the HR system, manager approves within 2 business days), and audience (all full-time employees).

ChatGPT returns a plain-language policy stating the 3-day limit, the approval requirement, and the core-hours rule; a process section describing the HR-system request and 2-day approval window; and a "Needs legal/compliance review" section flagging that jurisdiction-specific remote-work tax or labor requirements weren't addressed and should be checked before publishing, rather than inventing generic compliance language to fill that gap.

Tobias doesn't know exactly what to ask legal, so he sends the follow-up: "Look again at everything under 'Needs legal/compliance review' and phrase each as a direct question I can send our legal contact." ChatGPT turns the flag into a specific question: "Are there any state-specific requirements around remote work arrangements for employees working from a different state than our registered office?"

Tobias sends that exact question to the company's legal counsel before publishing anything. Once legal confirms there's nothing additional needed for their current employee locations, he fills in the real effective date, does a final read-through, and publishes the reviewed version — not the raw first draft. Total time: about 15 minutes, plus the time waiting on legal's answer before publishing.

placeholders.name: LIST YOUR REAL STAGES, e.g., requisition approval, job description drafting, sourcing/outreach, CV screening, phone screen, panel interview, hiring decision, offer, onboarding kickoff
placeholders.what: Your company's actual hiring stages, in the real order they happen — not a generic template. Some companies skip a requisition-approval step, or have two interview rounds instead of one; the map is only useful if it reflects how hiring genuinely works at your company.
examples: requisition approval, JD drafting, sourcing outreach, CV screening, recruiter phone screen, hiring manager interview, panel interview, reference checks, hiring decision, offer, background check, onboarding kickoff

role approval, JD drafting, internal referral window (first 2 weeks), external sourcing, resume screening, phone screen, take-home assessment, final panel, hiring decision, offer negotiation, onboarding
headcount approval, JD drafting, sourcing/outreach, CV screening, phone screen, skills assessment, panel interview, hiring decision, offer, onboarding kickoff

variations.label: Single-stage deep dive instead of the whole workflow
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you don't need the full end-to-end map yet and just want to carefully classify and build a template for one specific, higher-risk stage first, like CV screening.
variations.prompt:
Help me deeply classify and build a safe AI-assisted approach for just one stage of our hiring process, before I map the whole workflow.

Stage: [e.g. CV screening, interview question prep, offer letter drafting]
What currently happens at this stage, in detail: [DESCRIBE]

Classify it as "AI-assisted drafting," "AI-assisted summary/triage," or "human-only," with a clear reason. If this stage involves advancing or rejecting a candidate in any way, it must be classified as "AI-assisted summary/triage" at most — never AI-decided. Flag if this stage needs legal/compliance sign-off before using AI at all. Then draft a standing prompt template for this specific stage, including the guardrail that a human makes the final call, and a short QA checklist for testing it before relying on it for a real candidate.

variations.label: Compliance-focused audit of an existing (already in-use) AI workflow
variations.whenToUse: Use this when your team is already using AI somewhere in hiring without a formal map, and you need to audit current practice rather than design from a blank slate — useful before a compliance review.
variations.prompt:
I want to audit how our team is currently using AI in hiring, not design a new process from scratch.

Our real hiring stages, in order: [LIST YOUR REAL STAGES]
How AI is actually being used at each stage today, as far as I know: [DESCRIBE CURRENT PRACTICE PER STAGE, INCLUDING ANY YOU'RE UNSURE ABOUT]

For each stage, tell me: (1) whether current practice matches a safe classification (AI-assisted drafting / AI-assisted summary-triage / human-only) or has drifted into something riskier, (2) specifically what's risky about any stage that has drifted, particularly anything close to AI making an actual advance/reject/hire decision, (3) a concrete fix for any stage that needs one. Flag anything requiring immediate legal/compliance attention separately from lower-urgency items.

variations.label: Small-team / solo-recruiter simplified version
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a small company or a solo recruiter/HR person who doesn't need a formal multi-stakeholder rollout process, just a personal reference to hold themselves to consistent guardrails.
variations.prompt:
I'm a solo recruiter/HR person at a small company. Help me build a simple personal reference for where I safely use AI in hiring, not a formal team rollout.

Our real hiring stages, in order: [LIST YOUR REAL STAGES]

For each stage, classify as "AI-assisted drafting," "AI-assisted summary/triage," or "human-only," with a one-sentence reason, following the rule that any stage involving candidate advancement or rejection is never AI-decided. Keep this simple and short enough that I'll actually refer back to it — a one-page reference, not a formal policy document. For each AI-assisted stage, give me one short standing prompt template I can reuse, each explicitly stating that I make the final call.

followUps.label: Double-check nothing crosses into AI making the actual decision
followUps.prompt: Go through every stage classified as 'AI-assisted summary/triage' again and confirm, for each one, that the language in both the classification and the standing prompt template makes it unambiguous that a human makes the actual advance/reject decision — not just that AI 'helps.' Tighten the wording anywhere it's ambiguous.

followUps.label: A stage got classified as more automated than it should be
followUps.prompt: I think [STAGE NAME] is classified as more AI-friendly than it should be given [REASON, e.g. "it directly determines who moves to the next round"]. Reclassify it more conservatively and explain what changes in the standing prompt template as a result.

followUps.label: Flag anything needing legal/compliance sign-off more specifically
followUps.prompt: For every stage flagged as needing legal/compliance sign-off, turn that into a specific question I could send to our legal or compliance contact, rather than a general flag — I want something concrete I can actually act on.

followUps.label: Build the rollout communication for the team
followUps.prompt: Now that the map and templates are finalized, draft a short message I can send to every interviewer and hiring manager (not just the recruiting team) explaining the workflow map in plain terms, emphasizing clearly that no AI tool is ever making an actual hiring decision.

hr-a1-structured-hiring-workflow-ai-safe.walkthrough:
Naomi manages recruiting operations at a 150-person company and realizes different hiring managers are using AI inconsistently — one uses it to help screen CVs and sometimes rejects candidates based purely on its summary, while another avoids AI entirely, including for low-risk tasks like drafting outreach messages.

She lists her company's real hiring stages in order: requisition approval, JD drafting, sourcing outreach, CV screening, recruiter phone screen, panel interview, hiring decision, offer, and onboarding kickoff.

In Claude, she pastes the workflow-classification prompt with her real stages. Claude classifies JD drafting and sourcing outreach as "AI-assisted drafting" since a human reviews and sends the output; CV screening as "AI-assisted summary/triage," with an explicit note that a human must make every advance/reject call; phone screen and panel interview as "human-only" for the live conversation itself; hiring decision and offer approval as "human-only"; and offer letter drafting as "AI-assisted drafting." Each comes with a one-sentence reason and a reusable prompt template.

Naomi is specifically worried about the CV-screening stage, since that's where the risky practice has been happening. She sends the follow-up: "Go through every 'AI-assisted summary/triage' stage again and confirm the language makes it unambiguous a human makes the actual decision — tighten anywhere it's ambiguous." Claude revises the CV-screening template to explicitly state, in bold, that the AI output is never a pass/fail verdict and must never be the sole basis for rejecting a candidate.

She reviews the finalized map with her legal contact, sets up a Claude Project containing it, and sends a short rollout message to every hiring manager and interviewer — not just recruiting — making the human-decision rule explicit. Total time: about 30 minutes across the mapping and legal review.
